subject: SOCIAL STUDIES
title: Historic Built Environments in the County
overview: Historic built environments are places people have built that help us remember the past. In this sub-strand you will learn about museums, monuments and cultural centres, find out which of them are in your county, explain why they matter, and take part in caring for them.

lessons.title: Museums, monuments and cultural centres
objectives: Explain what a historic built environment is.
Describe museums, monuments and cultural centres.
lessons.intro: A river is a natural feature. A museum beside that river is different: people designed it, built it and use it to keep stories and objects from the past. Places like that are historic built environments.
lessons.notes:
The built environment means the things people have made in a place: buildings, monuments, roads and centres. A historic built environment is one that matters because of the past. It may be old, or it may have been built to remember an important person, event or way of life.

This sub-strand studies three kinds.

### Museums
A museum is a place where objects from the past are kept, cared for and shown. You might see tools, clothes, pots, photographs, musical instruments or the remains of animals that lived long ago. Labels tell you what each object is and where it came from. Kenya has museums in different parts of the country, looked after so that learners and visitors can study the past. A museum is not a shop. You look and learn. You handle an object only when a guide says you may.

### Monuments
A monument is a structure built to remember a person or an event. It may be a statue, a pillar, a grave of an important person, or an old building kept because of what happened there. People visit a monument to remember, not to climb on it or write their names on it.

### Cultural centres
A cultural centre is a place where a community shows and practises its culture. You may see traditional crafts, hear songs and stories, watch dances, or look at artefacts such as baskets and stools. Some cultural centres are large buildings. Others are smaller community spaces. Both count if people use them to keep culture alive.

### What they are not
A new shop, an ordinary classroom and a bus stage are built environments, but they are not historic unless they are kept because of the past. A mountain is historic in the sense that it is old, but it was not built by people, so it belongs with physical features, not here.

Every county does not have the same famous sites. Your task is to know the three kinds well, so that you can recognise a museum, a monument or a cultural centre when you find one in your county.

keyWords.meaning: a place people have built that is kept because of the past
a place where objects from the past are kept and shown
a structure built to remember a person or an event
a place where people learn, show and practise the culture of a community

examples.problem: Sort these into historic built environments and other places: a museum, a river, a monument, a vegetable stall.
steps: A museum and a monument are built and linked to the past.
A river is natural. A vegetable stall is built but not historic.
examples.answer: Historic built environments: the museum and the monument. The river is a physical feature. The stall is an ordinary built place.

examples.problem: A community hall is used every week for traditional songs, dances and crafts. Which of the three kinds is it closest to?
steps: Culture is practised and shown there.

activity.title: Name the three kinds
materials: Pictures of museums, monuments and cultural activities
steps: Brainstorm places in the county that learners think are historic. Share the list, and mark items the class is not sure about.
Sort the pictures under Museum, Monument and Cultural centre.
Say one thing you would see or do in each kind of place.
Set aside any picture of a natural feature and explain why it belongs in a different sub-strand.

practice.question: What is a museum?
practice.answer: A place where objects from the past are kept and shown so that people can learn.

practice.question: What is a monument for?
practice.answer: To remember an important person or event.

practice.question: Why is a mountain not a historic built environment?
practice.answer: People did not build it. It is a physical feature.

summary: Historic built environments are places people built that matter because of the past.
The three kinds in this sub-strand are museums, monuments and cultural centres.
Natural features belong in a different study.

lessons.title: Finding historic places in your county
objectives: Use print, digital sources and adults to identify historic built environments in your county.
Record a visit or a reported visit with notes or photographs.
lessons.intro: Knowing what a museum is does not yet tell you whether there is one near your school. Finding the historic places in your county means searching, asking and writing down only what you can support.
lessons.notes:
Some counties have well-known museums or monuments. Some have a cultural centre in a town. Some have a local monument that mainly the people of that area know. A few learners may live far from any of the three. The method is the same: search, then record what you find.

### Where to look
- Ask your teacher, parents and guardians.
- Look in an approved textbook or a county guide for the words museum, monument and cultural centre.
- With an adult, use a digital search or a digital map for historic places in your county. Read the name of the county in the result so that you do not collect a place from another county by mistake.
- Ask a community leader, a faith leader or a museum guide if the class can.

Write a table with three columns: Kind, Name, Where it is. If a column stays empty, write "None found yet" rather than inventing a place.

### A visit or a virtual visit
If a historic place is near the school, the teacher may arrange a visit. On the visit:

- Take notes: the name, what you saw, who explained it, and one story about why it is historic.
- Take photographs only if photography is allowed.
- If someone who works there agrees, an adult may record a short conversation. Ask permission first. Do not record people in secret.
- Stay with the group and follow the rules of the place.

If a visit is not possible, invite a resource person to class, or study photographs and a short text the teacher provides. Write notes as if you were preparing a younger child to visit later.

### Respect while you enquire
People may feel strongly about a monument or a cultural place. Listen to their accounts. You can write "Mr X told us..." so that the class knows it is a person's account. Check names of places carefully before you put them on a display.

keyWords.meaning: an adult with useful knowledge who is invited to help the class
being allowed to do something, such as taking a photograph

examples.problem: A website describes a famous museum, but the page does not say it is in your county. Should you add it to your county list?
steps: The list is for your county.
A famous museum elsewhere stays off the list.
examples.answer: No. Add it only if a reliable source shows that it is in your county.

activity.title: Search and record
materials: A digital device if the school has one and an adult is present
steps: Brainstorm and share the historic built environments learners already know.
Check the list with a print or digital resource and with the teacher.
Complete the table: kind, name and where it is. Write "None found yet" if you cannot confirm one.
If you visit a place, take notes and allowed photographs. If you cannot visit, record what a resource person or a text tells you.

practice.question: Name two sources you can use to identify historic built environments in your county.
practice.answer: Any two: teacher, parents, textbook, digital search with an adult, a community leader or a guide.

practice.question: What should you write if the class cannot confirm a monument in the county?
What must you do before recording a conversation at a historic place?
practice.answer: Ask permission. Do not record people in secret.

summary: Search with adults, books and careful digital sources.
Record only places you can locate in your county.
On a visit, take notes and ask before you photograph or record.

lessons.title: Why historic built environments are important
objectives: Explain the importance of museums, monuments and cultural centres.
Connect those reasons to a place in your county or to a place you have studied.
lessons.intro: Objects in a museum could have been thrown away. A monument could have been knocked down for a new building. Communities keep these places because they do jobs that a new shop cannot do.
lessons.notes:
Historic built environments are important for learning, for memory, for culture and for the living community around them.

### Learning
Museums let you see real objects instead of only hearing a description. A hoe, a coin or a photograph raises questions: Who used this? What was life like? School groups visit so that history becomes something they can look at. Guides and labels help you read the object correctly.

### Memory
Monuments remind the community of a person or an event. Remembering can mean honouring someone who served others, or remembering a hard time so that people treat one another better. When you stand quietly at a monument, you show that the memory matters.

### Culture
Cultural centres keep songs, dances, crafts and stories in use. Culture that is only talked about can be forgotten. Culture that is practised can be passed to children. Visitors from another community learn respect when they watch and listen.

### The community today
These places can bring visitors. Visitors may buy food, use transport and need guides, so some families earn a living. The places also give local people pride in their home area. A county that looks after its museum or cultural centre is saying that its past is part of its future.

If your table from the last lesson names a real place, choose that place and complete three sentences:

- This place is important for learning because...
- It is important for memory or culture because...
- It is important for people living here now because...

If your county list is still empty, use a museum, monument or cultural centre you have studied in a book, and say clearly that it is an example from Kenya, not a claim about your county. Then keep looking, with your family, for a local place.

A resource person, such as a guide, a curator or an elder, can add reasons you did not think of. Thank them, and write their points in your own words.

keyWords.meaning: a person who looks after the objects in a museum
keeping a person or an event in mind so they are not forgotten

examples.problem: Give two reasons a cultural centre is important.
steps: Think of culture being practised, and of the community today.
examples.answer: It keeps songs, dances and crafts alive, and it can teach visitors to respect the community. It may also support local work.

activity.title: Importance discussion
materials: A resource person if the teacher has invited one
steps: Choose one historic built environment from your county list, or a studied example if the list is empty.
Discuss its importance for learning, for memory or culture, and for people today.
If a resource person is present, ask why the place matters and how young people should behave there.
Share three points with the class and listen to the other groups.

practice.question: Give one reason museums are important for learning.
practice.answer: They keep and show real objects from the past so that people can study them.

practice.question: What does a monument help a community to do?
practice.answer: Remember an important person or event.

practice.question: Why should you say so if your example is not in your county?
practice.answer: So that you do not pretend your county has a place it may not have.

summary: Museums support learning, monuments support memory, and cultural centres keep culture alive.
These places can also help the local community.
Tie your reasons to a real local place, or label an example honestly.

lessons.title: Caring for historic places
objectives: Describe conservation activities for historic built environments.
Take part in a service activity that practises those habits.
lessons.intro: A monument does not stay clean and safe by itself. Wind, rain, litter and careless visitors all damage it. Conservation means the actions we take so that the place will still be there for younger children.
lessons.notes:
To conserve a historic built environment is to protect it from damage and dirt and to use it in a way that does not destroy it. Grade 4 learners can do real conservation work, especially the simple work of keeping a place clean and following rules.

### On a visit
- Do not write or scratch your name on walls, statues or benches.
- Do not climb on monuments.
- Do not touch objects in a museum unless the guide invites you.
- Do not pick plants that are part of the grounds if the rules say to leave them.
- Stay on the paths.
- Speak quietly so that other visitors can learn.
- Put litter in a bin. If there is no bin, carry the litter back with you.
- Report damage to the guide, a teacher or a parent. Do not try to repair an old object yourself.

### Service learning near you
Service learning means you help the community and learn while you help. With your teacher, choose a safe place:

- The compound of a nearby monument, museum or cultural centre, if the people in charge agree.
- If none of these is near, the school compound, while you practise the same habits you would use at a historic place.

Collect litter, sweep paths and wipe a display board if you are asked. Wear gloves if they are provided, wash your hands afterwards, and do not pick up broken glass or anything sharp. An adult supervises.

After the work, write three sentences: what you did, how it helps the place, and what you will remind a visitor to do. Conservation is not a one-day event. The habits continue every time you visit.

Working together on a clean-up also builds unity. Share the tools, take a fair area each, and thank the people who look after the place all year.

keyWords.meaning: to protect something so that it is not damaged or lost
helping the community while you learn from the work

examples.problem: You see a friend about to scratch a name on a monument. What should you do?
steps: Scratching damages the monument.
Ask them to stop, and tell an adult if they do not.
examples.answer: Ask them to stop. If they continue, tell the guide, your teacher or another adult.

examples.problem: There is no museum near your school. How can you still practise conservation?
steps: The same habits can be practised in the school compound.
examples.answer: Collect litter and sweep the school compound, and learn the rules you would follow on a visit.

activity.title: Service clean-up
materials: Water and soap for washing hands
steps: With your teacher, choose a historic place whose caretakers have agreed, or choose the school compound.
Divide the ground so that every group has an area.
Collect litter and sweep. Leave sharp objects for an adult.
Wash your hands.
Write what you did and one rule you will follow on a future visit.

practice.question: What does it mean to conserve a historic place?
practice.answer: To protect it from damage and dirt so that people can still use it in the future.

practice.question: Name two rules to follow inside a museum.
practice.answer: Any two: do not touch objects unless invited, do not write on walls, speak quietly, stay with the group, put litter in a bin.

practice.question: Why should learners not pick up broken glass on a clean-up?
practice.answer: Broken glass can cut them. An adult should deal with sharp objects.

summary: Conservation includes keeping places clean and not damaging them.
Collecting litter and sweeping are service-learning activities.
The same habits can be practised at school if a historic place is far away.

lessons.title: A picture booklet of places we value
objectives: Make a picture booklet about historic built environments.
Explain why you appreciate these places in your county.
lessons.intro: Appreciation grows when you can show someone else what a place is and why you would hate to see it spoiled. A small booklet does that job for your class.
lessons.notes:
To appreciate historic built environments is to value them as part of your county's story. You show appreciation by learning their names, speaking about them with respect, visiting them properly, and taking part in conservation.

### Make a picture booklet
Each group makes a booklet of four pages:

- Cover: the title "Historic places in our county", your group name, and a drawing.
- Page 1: a museum. If your county has one, draw it and write its name. If not, draw what a museum contains and write "We have not confirmed a museum in our county yet."
- Page 2: a monument, in the same honest way.
- Page 3: a cultural centre, in the same honest way.

On each page include:

- a drawing or an allowed photograph,
- the name and the kind of place,
- one sentence on why it is important,
- one sentence on how to care for it.

Use the notes from a visit, a resource person or a book. Do not copy a long text from a website. Write short sentences of your own.

### Tell the class
When you present the booklet, say what you appreciate. For example: "I appreciate our cultural centre because children learn the songs of our community there." If your pages are mostly "not confirmed yet", you can still appreciate the idea and describe how your class would behave on a visit. Honesty is part of respect.

Keep the booklets in the learning corner. Invite another class to look, and explain the pictures. At home, show the booklet to your family and ask whether they know a historic place you missed. Bring the name back, check it with your teacher, and add a page if it is confirmed.

Places that are cared for can still teach people when you are grown up. That is a strong reason to appreciate them now.

keyWords.meaning: to value a place and show that value in how you treat it
a few pages fastened together, with pictures and short writing

examples.problem: Your group cannot name a monument in the county. What should page 2 of the booklet say?
steps: Do not invent a monument.
You can still describe the kind of place and say it is not confirmed.
examples.answer: Write that the class has not confirmed a monument yet, and add a drawing of the kind of monument you have studied plus one care rule.

activity.title: Picture booklet
materials: Notes and allowed photographs from your search
steps: Fold or fasten four pages into a booklet.
Draw a museum, a monument and a cultural centre using your county list, and label any page you cannot confirm.
Add one importance sentence and one care sentence on each page.
Present the booklet and say what you appreciate.
Display the booklets and ask families if they know a confirmed place to add.

practice.question: What does it mean to appreciate a historic built environment?
practice.answer: To value it, learn about it, and treat it with respect and care.

practice.question: Name three things to put on a page of the picture booklet.
practice.answer: A drawing or photograph, the name and kind of place, why it is important, and how to care for it.

practice.question: Why is honesty important in the booklet?
practice.answer: Writing a place your county does not have would give the wrong information.

summary: A picture booklet shows museums, monuments and cultural centres honestly.
Each page gives an importance and a way to care.
Appreciation is shown by respect, learning and conservation.

quiz.question: Which set lists historic built environments from this sub-strand?
quiz.explanation: The three kinds are museums, monuments and cultural centres.

quiz.question: What is a museum?
options: A place where objects from the past are kept and shown
quiz.explanation: Museums keep objects so that people can learn about the past.

quiz.question: A hall used for traditional songs, dances and crafts is closest to a ___.
quiz.explanation: Cultural centres are where culture is shown and practised.

quiz.question: A famous museum is not said to be in your county. What should you do?
options: Add it to the county list anyway
Leave it off the county list until a reliable source places it in the county
Scratch its name on a wall
quiz.explanation: The county list should contain only places you can locate in the county.

quiz.question: Why are monuments important?
options: They remind people of a person or an event
They replace the need for schools
quiz.explanation: A monument is built for memory.

quiz.question: Give one reason cultural centres are important.
quiz.answer: They keep songs, dances, crafts or stories alive, or they help visitors respect the community.
quiz.explanation: Cultural centres pass culture on and can support community pride.

quiz.question: Which action is conservation?
options: Writing your name on a statue
Collecting litter and not climbing on a monument
quiz.explanation: Conservation protects a place from dirt and damage.

quiz.question: There is no historic place near your school. How can you still practise care?
quiz.answer: Collect litter and sweep the school compound, and learn the rules for a future visit.
quiz.explanation: Service learning can happen at school when a site is far away.

quiz.question: Before you record a guide's voice, you should ___.
Which sentence shows appreciation?
options: I value our cultural centre and I will help keep it clean.
I will invent a monument for the booklet.
I will scratch my name so people remember me.
quiz.explanation: Appreciation means valuing the place and caring for it.
